subject: algebra
problem:
Prove that for all positive real numbers $a,b,c,d$
$$\frac{a+b}{1+c}\cdot \frac{b+c}{1+d}\cdot \frac{c+d}{1+a}\cdot \frac{d+a}{1+b}\geq \frac{16abcd}{(1+\sqrt[4]{abcd})^4}.$$
proof:
The key observation is that 
 $$\frac{x+y}{(1+x)(1+y)}\geq \frac{2\sqrt{xy}}{(1+\sqrt{xy})^2}$$
 for all $x,y>0$. Indeed, writing this in the form 
 $$\frac{x+y}{2\sqrt{xy}}-1\geq \frac{1+x+y+xy}{(1+\sqrt{xy})^2}-1$$
 it becomes equivalent to
 $$\frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^2}{2\sqrt{xy}}\geq \frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^2}{(1+\sqrt{xy})^2},$$
 which is obvious. 
  Apply this observation twice, with $(x,y)=(a,b)$ and $(x,y)=(c,d)$. We obtain
  $$\frac{a+b}{1+c}\cdot \frac{b+c}{1+d}\cdot \frac{c+d}{1+a}\cdot \frac{d+a}{1+b}=\frac{a+b}{(1+a)(1+b)}\cdot 
  \frac{c+d}{(1+c)(1+d)}\cdot (b+c)(a+d)$$
  $$\geq \frac{4\sqrt{abcd}}{(1+\sqrt{ab})^2 (1+\sqrt{cd})^2}\cdot (\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{cd})^2,$$
  where we also use the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in the form $$(b+c)(a+d)\geq (\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{cd})^2.$$ It suffices therefore to prove that 
  $$\frac{\sqrt{ab}+\sqrt{cd}}{(1+\sqrt{ab})(1+\sqrt{cd})}\geq \frac{2\sqrt[4]{abcd}}{(1+\sqrt[4]{abcd})^2}.$$
  But this is yet another application of the key observation, with $x=\sqrt{ab}$ and $y=\sqrt{cd}$.

subject: number theory
problem:
Let $n>1$ be an integer. Prove that $2n-1$ is a prime number if and only if
for any $n$ pairwise distinct positive integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots ,
a_n$ there exist $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots , n\}$ such that
\[\frac{a_i+a_j}{\gcd(a_i,a_j)} \geq 2n-1.\]
proof:
Suppose first that $p=2n-1$ is a prime and let $a_1,...,a_n$ be pairwise distinct positive integers.
Suppose that \[\frac{a_i+a_j}{\gcd(a_i,a_j)}<p\] for $i,j\in
\{1,...,n\}$. Dividing each of the numbers $a_1,...,a_n$ by
$\gcd(a_1,...,a_n)$, we may assume that $\gcd(a_1,...,a_n)=1$.

If there is $i$ such that $p\mid a_i$, then we can choose
$j$ such that $p$ does not divide $a_j$ and then $p$ does not divide
$\gcd(a_i, a_j)$. Thus $p$ divides $\frac{a_i}{\gcd(a_i, a_j)}$ and
we obtain the plain contradiction
$$p\leq \frac{a_i}{\gcd(a_i, a_j)}<\frac{a_i+a_j}{\gcd(a_i,a_j)}<p.$$

Suppose now that $a_1,a_2,...,a_n$ are not multiples of $p$.
By the pigeonhole principle, two of the numbers
$a_1,a_2,...,a_n, -a_1,...,-a_n$ must give the same remainder when
divided by $p$. So we can find $i\ne j$ such that $p\mid a_i+a_j$ or
$p\mid a_i-a_j$. Note that $p$ does not divide $\gcd(a_i, a_j)$, so
$p$ divides $\frac{a_i\pm a_j}{\gcd(a_i, a_j)}$ for a suitable
choice of the sign $\pm$. We obtain again a contradiction
$$p>\frac{a_i+a_j}{\gcd(a_i, a_j)}\geq |\frac{a_i\pm a_j}{\gcd(a_i, a_j)}|\geq p.$$
So our initial assumption was wrong and the result follows.

Suppose now that $2n-1$ is composite, so we can write it as $xy$, with
$x,y>1$. Define $n$ integers $a_1,a_2,...,a_n$ by choosing the first
$x$ positive integers $1,2,...,x$, then the next $n-x$ even numbers
$x+1, x+3,..., xy-x$. It is not difficult to check that
$\frac{a_i+a_j}{\gcd(a_i, a_j)}<2n-1$ for all $i,j$.

subject: combinatorics
problem:
Let $\varepsilon>0$. Prove that for all but finitely many positive integers 
$n$, a graph with $n$ vertices and at least $(1+\varepsilon)n$ edges 
has two different cycles of equal length.
proof:
Suppose that $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices and at least $(1+\varepsilon)n$ edges. For simplicity,
suppose that $G$ is connected and pick a spanning tree $T$.
For each edge $e$ of $G$ not in $T$, adding $e$ produces a unique cycle 
$C_e$ and these $C_e$ have pairwise distinct lengths by assumption. 

Double count pairs $(f,e)$ where $e\in E(G)\setminus E(T)$ and 
$f\in E(C_e)\setminus \{e\}$. In particular $f\in E(T)$. 
For $f\in E(T)$ let $$X_f=\{e\in E(G)\setminus E(T)|\, f\in E(C_e)\setminus \{e\}\}.$$
Given $e\in E(G)\setminus E(T)$ there are $\text{length}(C_e)-1$ such $f$, thus 
$$\sum_{f\in E(T)} |X_f|\geq \sum_{e\in E(G)\setminus E(T)} (\text{length}(C_e)-1).$$
Since $|E(G)\setminus E(T)|\geq (1+\varepsilon)n-(n-1)>\varepsilon n$ and 
the lengths of the $C_e$'s are pairwise distinct, we obtain 
$$\sum_{f\in E(T)} |X_f|> \varepsilon^2 n^2/2.$$
Since $T$ has less than $n$ edges, it follows that there is 
$f\in E(T)$ such that $|X_f|> \varepsilon^2 n/2$. 

Take two different edges $e,e'\in X_f$. Look at the paths in $T$ between the endpoints of 
$e$ and $e'$. These paths share the edge $f$. One easily constructs a cycle containing the edges 
$e,e'$ and all of whose other edges are in $T$. In particular the cycles associated to different pairs of edges in $X_f$ are distinct and so 
$\binom{|X_f|}{2}\leq C$, where $C$ is the total number of cycles in $G$.

But any cycle in $G$ has at most $n$ vertices, so length $\leq n$, and there are no cycles of equal length, so $C\leq n$. We conclude that $n\geq \binom{ \lfloor \varepsilon^2 n/2\rfloor}{2}$ and this fails for $n$ big enough. This solves the problem for a connected graph. In general, simply take a spanning tree in each connected component and replace $T$ by the disjoint union of these trees. The rest of the argument goes through.

subject: geometry
problem:
Let $A_1\ldots A_n$ be a cyclic convex polygon whose circumcenter lies strictly inside the polygon and let $B_1,\ldots, B_n$ points on the sides $A_1A_2,\ldots, A_nA_1$ other than the vertices of the polygon. Prove that 
$$\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{B_iB_{i+1}}{A_iA_{i+2}}>1.$$
proof:
Let $R$ be the circumradius of the polygon $P=A_1\ldots A_n$ and let $R_i$ be the circumradius of triangle $B_iA_{i+1}B_{i+1}$. Since 
 $$B_iB_{i+1}=2R_i \sin A_{i+1},\,\, A_iA_{i+2}=2R\sin A_{i+1},$$
 the inequality is equivalent to 
 $$R_1+\ldots+R_n>R.$$
 Note that 
 $$B_iA_{i+1}+A_{i+1}B_{i+1}\leq 2R_i+2R_i=4R_i,$$
 thus it suffices to prove that 
 $$B_1A_2+A_2B_2+B_2A_3+A_3B_3+\ldots+B_nA_1+A_1B_1>4R,$$
 or equivalently the perimeter of $P$ is greater than four times $R$. We will prove this for any convex polygon inscribed in a circle of radius $R$, such that the center of the circle is inside the polygon. Partition the polygon into $n-2$ triangles using the diagonals
 $A_1A_3, A_1A_4,\ldots, A_1A_{n-1}$. By assumption for some $i$ the center $O$ of the circle is inside or on the boundary of triangle $A_1A_iA_{i+1}$. Note that the perimeter of the polygon is at least that of triangle $A_1A_iA_{i+1}$, since 
 $A_1A_2+\ldots+A_{i-1}A_i\geq A_1A_i$ and similarly $A_{i+1}A_{i+2}+\ldots+A_nA_1\geq A_{i+1}A_1$. Thus it suffices to prove that for a right or acute triangle inscribed in a circle of radius $R$ the perimeter is greater than $4R$. The case of a right triangle is trivial: if angle $B$ is $\pi/2$ then $AC=2R$ and so $AB+BC+CA>2AC=4R$. Suppose that $ABC$ is acute and let 
 $A_1,B_1,C_1$ be the midpoints of the sides $BC, CA, AB$. Then $O$ is the orthocenter of $A_1B_1C_1$ and it lies inside this triangle. If the line $C_1O$ intersects the segment $A_1B_1$ at $S$, then 
 $$AB+BC+CA=2(AA_1+A_1B_1+B_1C)=2(AA_1+A_1S)+2(SB_1+B_1C)>$$
 $$2AS+2SC>2AO+2CO=4R,$$
 where we used that the angles $AOS$ and $COS$ are obtuse.

subject: number theory
problem:
Find all arithmetic progressions $a_{1},a_{2},...$ of positive integers for which there is an integer $N>1$ such that for all
$k\geq 1$ $$a_{1}a_{2}...a_{k}\mid a_{N+1}a_{N+2}...a_{N+k}.$$
proof:
Write $a_n=a+nd$ for $n\geq 1$ and some $d\geq 1$. If $a=0$, then the sequence $(a_n)_n$ is a solution of the problem, since
the product of $k$ consecutive integers is a multiple of $k!$. We will prove that the case $a>0$ is impossible. Dividing $a$ and $d$ by their greatest common divisor, we may assume that
$\gcd(a,d)=1$. For $k>N$ by dividing the divisibility relation by $a_{N+1}...a_k$ we obtain
$$a_1a_2...a_N\mid a_{k+1}a_{k+2}...a_{k+N}.$$
Since
$a_1a_2...a_N>N!$, there is a prime $p$ such that
$v_p(a_1...a_N)>v_p(N!)$. Then $p$ divides at least one of the numbers
$a_1,...,a_N$, and these are all relatively prime to $d$ since $\gcd(a,d)=1$. Thus
$p$ does not divide $d$ and so there is an integer $k>N$ such that
$p^{v_p(a_1...a_N)}\mid a_k=a+dk$. But then $v_p(a_k)>v_p(N!)\geq v_p(jd)$ for $1\leq j\leq N$, hence
\begin{align*}
v_p(N!)
& <v_p(a_1...a_N)\leq v_p(a_{k+1}...a_{k+N})\\
& =v_p((a_k+d)(a_k+2d)...(a_k+Nd))\\
& =v_p(a_k+d)+v_p(a_k+2d)+...+v_p(a_k+Nd)\\
& =v_p(d)+v_p(2d)+...+v_p(Nd)=v_p(N!),
\end{align*}
a contradiction.

subject: geometry
problem:
The $100\times 100$ square unit lattice $\textbf{L}$ has $10000$ points. A set $\mathcal{F}$ of polygons has the property that the set of vertices of the union of all polygons in $\mathcal{F}$ is exactly 
$\textbf{L}$. Find the maximum possible sum of the areas of the polygons in $\mathcal{F}$.
proof:
The answer is $\frac{n^2(4n^2-1)}{3}$ for a $2n \times 2n$ grid. Let $O$ be the center of the grid. For any polygon $A_1A_2 \cdots A_n$, the area
\[[A_1A_2 \cdots A_n] \leq \sum_{i=1}^n OA_i \cdot OA_{i+1} \leq \sum_{i=1}^n \frac 12\left(OA_i^2 + OA_{i+1}^2\right)  = \sum_{i=1}^n OA_i^2\]by the sine area formula. Summing this across all points in the grid yields $$\sum_{F \in \mathcal F} [F] \leq \sum_{P \in \mathbf L} OP^2,$$ which is sharp when all the polygons $P$ are squares. Note that 
$$ \sum_{P \in \mathbf L} OP^2=4\sum_{0\le i,j\le n-1}((i+0.5)^2+(j+0.5)^2)\cdot(1/\sqrt2)^2=\frac{n^2(4n^2-1)}3.$$
 To achieve the bound it suffices to consider squares with center at $O$, i.e. a spiral of squares, for the outermost layer have the biggest square, and then a square formed by moving each vertex 1 point counterclockwise, and continue doing that until the outer layer is finished.
